Pradeep, a final-year student, told me on Wednesday that an uncle had asked him to come home for the whole week of a family wedding and skip his lab project deadline. When he said he could not, the uncle told him he only thought of himself. Pradeep said the words stayed with him all night, and he admitted he was tempted to say yes just to make it stop.
I did not tell him what to do. We talked about which parts he could offer. On Friday he phoned his uncle and calmly said he could not miss the deadline, but he would come on Saturday and help with the guest list. The uncle went quiet, then agreed. Pradeep looked lighter when he told me.

qa.q: What did the uncle ask Pradeep to do for the wedding?
qa.a: The uncle asked him to come home for the whole week of the family wedding and skip his lab project deadline.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling after being told he only thought of himself?
qa.a: Pradeep felt hurt and pressured, since the words stayed with him all night and he was tempted to say yes just to make it stop.

qa.q: What did Pradeep choose to do on Friday, and why was it a fair way to answer?
qa.a: He calmly told his uncle he could not miss the deadline but offered to come on Saturday and help with the guest list, which set a limit and still gave support.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have seen Pradeep's call to the uncle?
qa.a: Amandeep seems to have seen it as a good step, noting that Pradeep looked lighter afterwards, and had left the choice to Pradeep by not telling him what to do.

grounding: A young adult who declines a family demand is called selfish, and calmly explaining limits and offering help elsewhere is fairer.
